reagents.name: Lead(II) nitrate solution, 0.3 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of solid lead nitrate, the pure substance, from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H272: May intensify fire; oxidizer
H302+H332: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled
H318: Causes serious eye damage
H350: May cause cancer
H360: May damage fertility or the unborn child
H373: May cause damage to organs through prolonged or repeated exposure
H410: Very toxic to aquatic life with long lasting effects

note.value:
The solution on this bench is 0.3 mol/L lead nitrate. The same supplier's sheet for the solution drops three of the statements above: the fire hazard, the damage to the eyes and the code for water life. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and a fume hood or a well-ventilated room.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for a stronger solution, 0.5 M, adds H320, it irritates the eyes, and has H410: it is kept out of drains and waterways. Eyes are flushed for 15 minutes or more and a doctor is seen at once; if any is swallowed, a doctor or a poison centre at once. It says that lead builds up in the body. A third's sheet for the solid adds a skin allergy.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Hydrochloric acid, 0.3 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of concentrated hydrochloric acid (6 M to 12 M), from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314+H318: Causes severe skin and eye burns and damage
H332+H302: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value:
The acid on this bench is 0.3 mol/L hydrochloric acid; the statements above are those of the concentrated acid it is made from. The same supplier's sheet for this strength keeps Danger and H314, and has H335: it may irritate the airways. It calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and a fume hood or a well-ventilated room; splashed clothing comes off at once.

Stricter, and what this lab goes by: a second supplier's sheet for a 0.5 M solution classes it more mildly, as an irritant, and asks more at the eyewash: eyes are flushed for 15 minutes or more and a doctor is seen at once. NOAA's record adds 15 minutes more where no doctor has come. The acid is kept from bases and from metals, with which it gives off hydrogen.

How any of it is disposed of is decided by the laboratory's own rules and by local regulations; ask the laboratory's supervisor.

reagents.name: Hydrochloric acid, 6 M
reagents.classifiedAs: Hazards of concentrated hydrochloric acid (6 M to 12 M), from a supplier's safety data sheet

statements: H314+H318: Causes severe skin and eye burns and damage
H332+H302: Harmful if swallowed or inhaled
H290: May be corrosive to metals

note.value: The acid on this bench is 6 mol/L, which is about 20% hydrogen chloride by mass (worked out from the molarity and a density of about 1.1 g/mL, not read from a source). The sheet the statements above come from is for acid of 6 M to 12 M, so it covers this acid, the least concentrated it is for, and the statements apply to it as they stand. The sheet gives the signal word Danger and three statements: under H314 and H318, that the acid burns the skin and the eyes severely and damages them; under H332 and H302, that it is harmful if it is swallowed or breathed in; and under H290, that it may corrode metals. The sheet calls for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and for working in a fume hood or a well-ventilated room, and says that the mist, the vapour or the spray of the acid is not to be breathed. It says that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. It says that a splash in the eyes is to be rinsed with water for several minutes, with contact lenses taken out if that is easily done, and the rinsing then kept up. After a splash on the skin or the hair, it says, the wet clothing is to come off at once and the skin be rinsed with water.

Both give the signal word Danger and, under the code H314, the statement that the solution burns the skin severely and damages the eyes. The sheet that begins at 6.1 M adds a second statement, under H290: the solution may corrode metals. Handle this solution as the stricter sheet says, the one that begins at 6.1 M. Both sheets call for eye protection, gloves and protective clothing, and say that the mist, the vapour or the spray of the solution is not to be breathed. Both say that a poison centre or a doctor is to be called at once. substances.name: Methyl violet, the form that holds a hydrogen ion
Methyl violet, the form that has given up a hydrogen ion
Cobalt ion with six water molecules
Cobalt ion with four chloride ions
Zinc ion with four hydroxide ions
Zinc ion with four ammonia molecules

rules.says: Chloride ions bring lead ions out of a solution as white solid lead chloride, once the liquid holds more of the two than it can keep dissolved. The model puts that point where the concentration of lead times the square of the concentration of chloride passes what it is in water saturated with lead chloride alone.
Hot water holds over three times as much lead chloride as cold water, so the solid dissolves when the tube is heated and comes back when it is cooled. Dissolving lead chloride takes in heat.
Water added to the tube lowers the concentration of both ions, and the solid dissolves once the liquid holds no more of them than it can keep dissolved.

Methyl violet is yellow at pH 0.0 and below and changes colour between pH 0.0 and pH 1.6. In water with no acid in it, it is violet. Inside the range both forms are in the liquid, and the colour seen is a mixture.
A hydrogen ion and a hydroxide ion join into a molecule of water. So sodium hydroxide takes hydrogen ions out of a liquid, and an acid takes hydroxide ions out of one, one for one.

In concentrated hydrochloric acid, cobalt is held as a blue ion with four chloride ions. Water turns it back into the pink ion with six water molecules. Where both ions are in the liquid together, the liquid is violet.
A liquid that holds both cobalt ions turns blue in hot water and pink in ice water: the change toward the blue ion takes in heat.
Sodium hydroxide brings zinc ions and magnesium ions out of a solution as white solid hydroxides.
An acid takes hydroxide ions away as water, and a solid hydroxide dissolves to replace them.
Zinc hydroxide dissolves in an excess of sodium hydroxide: a zinc ion with four hydroxide ions is a complex ion, which stays dissolved.
Zinc hydroxide dissolves in an excess of ammonia: a zinc ion with four ammonia molecules is a complex ion, which stays dissolved.

Magnesium hydroxide dissolves in neither an excess of sodium hydroxide nor an excess of ammonia. Magnesium rarely forms complex ions and forms none that would hold it dissolved in either, and each of them brings magnesium hydroxide down.

note.value: The two figures are one page's, for 20 °C and for 100 °C, and are for lead chloride alone in water. This tube also holds lead nitrate, with far more lead in it than chloride. The model takes the same product of the two concentrations to mark saturation there, which leaves out what the other ions in the liquid do. One procedure read sees no solid at a mixture where this product says there is one, so a real bench may need more acid than this lab does.

The table read gives the change as yellow to blue over the range, and the procedure read calls the indicator in water violet. The model has three looks: yellow at the bottom of the range and below it, a colour between blue and yellow inside it, and violet where no acid is left. It has none for a liquid above the range with a little acid still in it, which the table has as blue, and the build checks that no such liquid is reached.

systems.name: A solid and its ions: lead chloride

notes.value: Hydrochloric acid brought chloride ions, which are on the left side. After the first portion the liquid could still hold all of its lead and chloride ions, so nothing was seen. The second portion took the tube past that point, and the extra came out as white solid lead chloride: a shift to the right.
On a real bench lead chloride is slow to form. The solid can take some minutes to show, and may need more acid than it does here.
Hot water holds over three times as much lead chloride as cold water. In the boiling bath all of the solid dissolved: a shift to the left, toward the ions.
Dissolving lead chloride takes in heat, about 23 kJ for each mole. Heating a system at equilibrium moves it the way that takes heat in, which here is toward the ions.

Cooling took heat away, and the system moved the way that gives heat out: toward the solid. The cold liquid could no longer hold all of the lead chloride, and the white solid came back: a shift to the right.

Water spread the same ions through more liquid, so both concentrations fell. They fell below what the liquid can hold, and the solid dissolved: a shift to the left. Diluting a solution moves an equilibrium toward the side with more dissolved particles, and here that side is the ions.
Hydrochloric acid added hydrogen ions, which are on the right side. The system used some of them up: they joined the violet form and made more of the yellow form. That is a shift to the left.
After the first portion both forms were in the liquid together. The colour was a mixture, neither violet nor yellow.

Each hydroxide ion joined a hydrogen ion and made water. That took hydrogen ions away from the right side. The yellow form let go of hydrogen ions to replace them and became the violet form again: a shift to the right.

Water is on the right side of this equilibrium. Adding it turned the blue ion, cobalt with four chloride ions, back into the pink ion, cobalt with six water molecules: a shift to the left. After the first portion both ions were there together, and the liquid was violet.

Concentrated hydrochloric acid gives off heat when water is added to it, so a real tube warms. Warmth moves this system toward blue, against the water. This lab shows the tube once it is back at room temperature.
The change toward the blue ion takes in heat. Heating a system at equilibrium moves it the way that takes heat in, so in the boiling bath the liquid turned blue: a shift to the right.

In ice water the system moved the way that gives heat out, back toward the pink ion: a shift to the left. Heating and cooling undo each other here: the tube that was blue in the hot bath is pink in the cold one.

disturbances.name: Zinc, a drop of sodium hydroxide

notes.value: Sodium hydroxide brought hydroxide ions, which are on the left side. Zinc ions and hydroxide ions joined into white solid zinc hydroxide: a shift to the right.
One drop holds enough hydroxide for only half of the zinc in the tube. The other half is still dissolved, so the solid sits in a liquid that holds its own ions.

The hydrogen ions of the acid joined hydroxide ions and made water, which took hydroxide away from the left side. The solid came apart to replace it, until none of the solid was left: a shift to the left.

By the first equilibrium alone, more hydroxide should give more solid. But zinc has a second equilibrium. With plenty of hydroxide about, a zinc ion takes up four hydroxide ions and becomes a complex ion, which stays dissolved.
That took zinc ions out of the first equilibrium, and the solid dissolved to replace them. What took the zinc ion away was hydroxide itself.

Ammonia is a base, and makes a little hydroxide in water. But it also joins the zinc ion itself: one zinc ion and four ammonia molecules make a complex ion, which stays dissolved. That took zinc ions out of the first equilibrium, and the solid dissolved to replace them.
By this lab's numbers that takes a large excess of ammonia, eight times the volume of the tube, because the hydroxide set free as the solid dissolves holds the change back.

disturbances.name: Magnesium, a drop of sodium hydroxide

notes.value: Sodium hydroxide brought hydroxide ions, which are on the left side. Magnesium ions and hydroxide ions joined into white solid magnesium hydroxide: a shift to the right.
One drop holds enough hydroxide for only half of the magnesium in the tube. The other half is still dissolved, so the solid sits in a liquid that holds its own ions.

The hydrogen ions of the acid joined hydroxide ions and made water, which took hydroxide away from the left side. The solid came apart to replace it, until none of the solid was left: a shift to the left.

Magnesium has no second equilibrium to turn to: it forms no complex ion that would hold it dissolved in more hydroxide. More hydroxide only pushed the first equilibrium further to the right, and the white solid stayed. Nothing took the magnesium ion away.

Magnesium forms no complex ion with ammonia that would hold it dissolved, either. Here ammonia acted only as a base: it made hydroxide ions in the water, which keeps the first equilibrium to the right, and the white solid stayed.

temperatureKelvin.rationale: The temperature the table's Gibbs energies and enthalpies are for, 25 °C. Each constant is worked out at it, and used for a bench at room temperature.

dropMicrolitres.rationale: A drop from a dropper is taken as 0.05 mL, twenty to the millilitre, as the titration lab and the Group I cations lab take it. Every liquid on this bench is measured out as a count of drops.

boilingBathCelsius.rationale: A tube standing in the bath of boiling water is taken to be at 100 °C, the temperature the hot solubility of lead chloride is given for. A real tube is a little cooler.

coldCelsius.rationale: A tube at room temperature and a tube in the bath of ice water are both taken at 20 °C, the temperature the cold solubility of lead chloride is given for. By the two figures read, water holds less lead chloride the colder it is, so a solid that is there by the figure for 20 °C is taken to be there in ice water too.

clearOfEdge.rationale: No number decides a tube from the very edge of what it is compared with. At every stage where a number says whether a solid is there, or which colour the indicator has, the build checks that the number is at least this many times away from its threshold, and stops otherwise.

completeWithinPercent.rationale: The model takes one drop of sodium hydroxide to put all of its hydroxide into the solid. The build checks that the part of that hydroxide which the solubility product leaves dissolved, beside the metal ion still in the liquid, is under this share of what went in.

leadNitrateDrops.rationale: Thirty drops, 1.5 mL, of the 0.3 M solution: 450 micromoles of lead. The procedure read starts from 5 mL; this tube is smaller, so that a small portion of acid is still a whole number of drops.

leadAcidDrops.rationale: One portion of the 0.3 M acid is two drops: 30 micromoles of chloride. It is chosen with the thirty drops of lead solution so that, by the stored solubility, the first portion leaves the tube short of the point where a solid forms and the second takes it past, each by more than the build's margin. The procedure read adds the acid by the millilitre to 5 mL.

leadAcidPortions.rationale: Three portions: one that shows nothing, one that brings the solid, and one more, so that there is enough solid to watch dissolve and come back.

leadWaterDrops.rationale: Sixty drops, 3 mL, of distilled water: by the stored solubility, enough to take the tube well below the point where a solid is there. The procedure read adds water by the millilitre until the solid has gone.

indicatorWaterDrops.rationale: Twenty drops, 1 mL, of distilled water. The procedure read uses about 5 mL and a few drops of acid; this tube is smaller, so that a few whole drops of the 6 M acid take it all the way to the yellow end of the indicator's range.

indicatorDrops.rationale: Two drops of the indicator solution, where the procedure read says a few. They add their volume to the tube and nothing else: the indicator is taken to use up no acid.

indicatorPortionDrops.rationale: One portion of the 6 M acid, and one of the 6 M sodium hydroxide, is three drops: 900 micromoles. It is chosen so that one portion of acid leaves the liquid inside the indicator's range and two take it past the yellow end, each by more than the build's margin.

indicatorPortions.rationale: Two portions of acid and then two of sodium hydroxide. As much base as acid leaves no acid over, which is where the indicator is violet again. The model has no rule for a liquid with base left over, and the build checks that none is reached.

cobaltChlorideGrams.rationale: About 0.1 g of the solid, as the procedure read has it. No number of the model turns on it: the colours of this system are stored observations.

cobaltAcidDrops.rationale: Forty drops, 2 mL, of the 12 M acid, as the procedure read has it.

cobaltWaterDrops.rationale: One portion of water is forty drops, 2 mL, which is the volume of the acid. The procedure read adds 2 mL and then goes on by the millilitre until the colour changes.

cobaltWaterPortions.rationale: Two portions. The demonstration read has both ions together, and a violet liquid, where six tenths of the liquid is concentrated acid. The first portion here leaves half of the liquid acid, which the lab stores as violet; the second leaves a third, which it stores as pink.

metalNitrateDrops.rationale: Sixty drops, 3 mL, of the 0.1 M solution: 300 micromoles of the metal ion. The procedure read puts about 2 mL in each of three tubes; here one tube is made up and then shared.

firstBaseDrops.rationale: One drop of the 6 M sodium hydroxide, as the procedure read has it: 300 micromoles of hydroxide, which is enough for half of the metal ion. So half of it stays dissolved, and the solid lies in a liquid that holds its own ions.

shareDrops.rationale: Ten drops, 0.5 mL, of the stirred mixture go into each of three small tubes, and the amounts in a share are rounded to the whole nanomole. A small share keeps the ammonia of the third tube to an amount that a test tube holds.

hydroxideAcidDrops.rationale: One drop of the 6 M acid: 300 micromoles, about six times what the hydroxide of a share can take up.

excessBaseDrops.rationale: Twenty drops, 1 mL, of the 6 M sodium hydroxide. The build checks that, by the stored constants, this much holds all the zinc of a share dissolved as its complex ion, with room to spare.

ammoniaDrops.rationale: Eighty drops, 4 mL, of the 6 M ammonia: eight times the volume of a share. By the stored constants, zinc hydroxide that sodium hydroxide brought down needs about that much, because the hydroxide ions it sets free as it dissolves hold the change back. The procedure read adds ammonia a drop at a time until the solid is seen to change.
